card.title: QUININE
card.text: Target infantry gets +1+2 and -1 operation cost.
card.flavorText: Quinine was one of the most important anti-malaria drugs used by US forces in the Pacific during WWII. Jungle heat, heavy rains, swamps, mud, and mountain terrain made service difficult, but mosquitoes made it far worse. Malaria spread quickly in the South Pacific, often causing more casualties than combat itself, and weakening entire units before battle. The Army already knew basic prevention methods, including mosquito nets, careful camp placement, and regular quinine or Atabrine treatment. But in practice, supply shortages, long transport routes, and limited numbers of tropical diseases specialists made control difficult. Early estimates for anti-malaria supplies were far below real demand, and commanders warned that without enough quinine, many other supplies would lose much of their value. In the Philippines in 1942, about 24,000 of 75,000 American and Filipino defenders were estimated to be suffering from malaria. Across the South Pacific, many soldiers caught the disease at some point. Atabrine helped, but some men avoided it because it could turn skin yellow. Quinine remained a vital treatment when available, especially for troops already weakened by hunger, dysentery, and exhaustion.
